title: Trump Warns Iran "It's Time, One Way or Another, for You to Make a Deal" - Insists Negotiations Have Gone on "Continuously, Including Today" as Iranian Media Claims Talks Went Silent - NewsBreak
text:
By Rob Glenn ,
1 days ago
President Donald Trump forcefully rejected Iranian reports of a breakdown in diplomatic communications on Tuesday, declaring in a Truth Social post that U.S.-Iran negotiations had proceeded without interruption — even as Iranian state media sources said the two sides had gone silent for several days. The dueling accounts came as Secretary of State Marco Rubio testified before Congress for the first time since the United States entered the conflict with Iran, offering cautious optimism about nuclear talks while outlining Washington’s firm conditions for any deal.
Trump Fires Back at Iranian Media Reports In a post published to Truth Social around noon on June 2, Trump directly disputed accounts circulating in Iranian media suggesting the two sides had stopped communicating. “Fake News Reports that the Islamic Republic of Iran, and the U.S.A., stopped speaking a few days ago are false and erroneous,” Trump wrote. “The conversations between us have been going on continuously, including four days ago, three days ago, two days ago, one day ago, and today.”
Trump used the post to press Tehran on the urgency of reaching an agreement, invoking the long history of U.S.-Iran tensions. “Where they lead, one never knows, but as I told Iran, ‘It’s time, one way or another, for you to make a Deal. You’ve been doing this for 47 years, and it cannot be allowed to go on any longer!'” he wrote.
The remarks echoed statements Trump made the day prior. On Monday, the president told NBC News he believed negotiations were still within reach, while also suggesting he was prepared to wait Tehran out. “I think I can wait as long as they want,” Trump said, adding that going silent would not mean a return to full-scale military operations.
Iran’s Version of Events Iranian state media presented a starkly different picture. More than three months after the U.S. and Israel launched strikes against Iran, the conflict has been stuck in a stalemate, with a shaky ceasefire in place while the pivotal Strait of Hormuz remains largely shut to maritime traffic.
Iran’s semi-official Mehr News Agency cited a source saying Tehran had not yet responded to a proposed final text of a temporary deal, and was taking a “stern” approach given what it described as a long history of U.S. non-compliance. The semi-official Fars agency added that messages on a possible memorandum of understanding had ceased several days prior, with the last communication being Tehran’s position on Lebanon, where Iran is seeking an end to Israel’s incursion against its ally Hezbollah.
Iran is pushing for a limited interim agreement, seeking relief from mounting economic pressure while resisting major concessions on its nuclear program. Among Tehran’s stated conditions are an end to hostilities across all fronts, access to billions of dollars in frozen oil revenues, waivers on crude exports, a lifting of the U.S. port blockade, and continued leverage over the Strait of Hormuz.
Rubio Takes the Stand Secretary of State Marco Rubio appeared before the Senate Foreign Relations Committee for his first public testimony since U.S. and Israeli strikes against Iran began on February 28 , as Congress has grown increasingly uneasy over the war, its economic fallout, and questions about the administration’s long-term strategy.
Rubio struck a notably more optimistic tone on nuclear negotiations than Washington has offered in recent weeks. “They have agreed to negotiate aspects of their nuclear program that just a month ago, just a year ago, they were refusing to even mention,” he told lawmakers, while cautioning that it was “not a guarantee that ultimately it will lead to a deal that’s acceptable” by Congress. He added that the negotiations have been made difficult by the instability of Iran’s leadership.
Rubio further outlined what Iran would need to commit to before more detailed nuclear talks could proceed. “They have to commit to very specific negotiations on the disposition of the highly enriched uranium that still is buried deep in a mountain somewhere,” he said.
On the question of sanctions relief, Rubio was explicit that no concessions had been offered in exchange for reopening the strait. “Iran is being sanctioned because they’ve highly enriched uranium. Iran is being sanctioned because of their nuclear activities. If they agree to give up those things, there will be sanctions relief associated with their commitment and compliance with those agreements,” he said.
The Strait of Hormuz and the Economic Stakes The conflict has caused global pain by pushing up energy prices since Iran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz, which previously carried about a fifth of global supplies of oil and liquefied natural gas. Oil prices edged up to a one-week high on Tuesday.
Trump said on Monday that a deal to extend the ceasefire and reopen the strait was achievable within the coming week — a timeline he has cited repeatedly since mid-March without a breakthrough materializing. Trump faces competing pressures on the issue: the need to reopen global energy lanes and curb U.S. fuel prices, while avoiding what the administration would frame as capitulation to Tehran.
Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps reported on Tuesday that 24 vessels had transited the strait in the past 24 hours after obtaining permission from the Guards’ navy — an arrangement that underscores Tehran’s continued leverage over one of the world’s most critical shipping chokepoints. The IRGC also claimed responsibility for striking a vessel operated by the world’s largest shipping group, MSC, while docked at Iraq’s Umm Qasr port, calling it retaliation for a prior U.S. attack on an Iranian vessel in the Gulf of Oman.
Lebanon and the Wider Regional War The diplomatic tension over Iran unfolded alongside a deteriorating situation in Lebanon. I srael continued strikes on towns across southern Lebanon on Tuesday despite a U.S.-mediated partial ceasefire announced Monday, under which Israel would refrain from striking Beirut and Hezbollah-controlled suburbs while Hezbollah would halt attacks on Israel. The announcement offered little reassurance to many Lebanese civilians, 1.2 million of whom have been displaced.
President Trump announced major combat operations against Iran on February 28, with massive joint U.S.-Israeli strikes targeting military, government, and infrastructure sites. Following the announcement of a two-week ceasefire, initial U.S.-Iran talks in Pakistan in April failed to reach a peace deal, after which Trump announced an open-ended extension of the ceasefire alongside the continuation of a U.S. blockade until negotiations are concluded “one way or the other.”
The humanitarian toll of the wider conflict continues to mount. The U.N. children’s agency UNICEF warned Tuesday that surging transport costs and supply chain disruptions caused by the Strait of Hormuz closure are hindering life-saving aid from reaching Gaza, Lebanon, the Democratic Republic of Congo, Mali, Somalia, South Sudan, Nigeria, and elsewhere — a reminder of the far-reaching consequences of a conflict now entering its fourth month with no final resolution in sight.

Iran’s semi-official Mehr News Agency cited a source saying Tehran had not yet responded to a proposed final text of a temporary deal, and was taking a “stern” approach given what it described as a long history of U.S. non-compliance.
